cues.text: A Year of Three Popes
1978 became known, in the memory of the Church, as the "Year of Three Popes": Pope Paul VI died on August 6 after a fifteen-year pontificate.
That pontificate had guided the Church through the Second Vatican Council's implementation; his successor, John Paul I , elected in late August, died suddenly after only thirty-three days as pope.
This plunged the College of Cardinals into a second conclave within the same year, convened in October.
A Surprising Choice
On October 16, 1978, the assembled cardinals elected Karol Wojtyła , Archbishop of Kraków, Poland.
He was the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, since the Dutch pope Adrian VI in 1522, and the first Polish pope in the Church's entire history.

Wojtyła took the name John Paul II in honor of his immediate predecessor, and appeared on the loggia of St. Peter's Basilica to greet a crowd genuinely startled by the choice of a pope from behind the Iron Curtain.
A Pope Formed by Occupation and Communism
Wojtyła's own life had been shaped by decades of totalitarian rule: he had studied for the priesthood in a clandestine underground seminary during Poland's Nazi occupation.
He had spent his subsequent priestly and episcopal ministry navigating a Communist government's constraints and open hostility to religious practice.
This formative experience gave him, from the very outset of his pontificate, an unusually direct, personally tested understanding of the totalitarian systems then still dividing Europe.
Wojtyła's own father, a former army officer, raised him largely alone after the early deaths of his mother and only sister.
The future pope lost his elder brother, a physician, to scarlet fever when Karol was still a young man.
Friends and biographers have long connected these personal losses to the depth of his later pastoral sensitivity to grief and suffering.
"Be Not Afraid"
In his inaugural homily on October 22, 1978, John Paul II addressed the whole Church, and the wider world, with words that would define the spirit of his pontificate: "Be not afraid!
Open wide the doors for Christ."
His first pilgrimage to his native Poland the following year, in 1979, drew crowds of millions despite discouragement from the Communist authorities.
Historians widely credit the visit with galvanizing the Solidarity movement that would, within a decade, help bring down Communist rule across Eastern Europe.
Legacy
John Paul II went on to lead the Church for over twenty-six years, the third-longest pontificate in history.
He became the most-traveled pope ever, canonized more saints than all his predecessors combined, and survived an assassination attempt in 1981.
He personally visited and forgave its perpetrator in prison.
Canonized himself in 2014, John Paul II remains, for many, simply "John Paul the Great."
His election from the very Communist world he would help to dismantle stands as one of the most consequential in modern papal history.
